Inscriptible Quadri

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four lines that just touch a circle make a shape whose opposite sides add up the same.
How to play: Drag the four dots on the circle, or drag its middle. Focus a dot and use the arrow keys too; tick the boxes to show the names, dots, tangents and sides.

Drag a dot round the circle, or drag the grey centre to move the whole picture (Shift for bigger arrow-key steps).

Look for the math

Drag any dot and the four-sided shape changes shape completely, yet two totals keep matching. Here is the small trick that makes that unavoidable.

Lines that just touch

A tangent meets the circle at right angles to the radius there. From one corner, the two tangents to the circle have equal lengths: the two right triangles share the radius and the line from the corner to the centre, so their third sides match. In the picture that says AP = AM, BP = BN, CN = CQ and DQ = DM. The logic test checked these four equalities on 2,496 random arrangements; the largest scaled difference was below 1e-11.

Adding the pieces

Each side is two of those equal pieces: AB = AP + PB, BC = BN + NC, CD = CQ + QD and DA = DM + MA. So AB + CD = (AM + BN) + (CN + DM) = (AM + DM) + (BN + CN) = DA + BC. That is Pitot's theorem, exactly the claim printed on the page: AB + CD = BC + DA. The test confirmed it on 2,808 random inscribed pictures and 560 placements on a grid of angles, to floating-point precision.

The converse, and when the circle moves out

The page adds that the usual proof of the converse has a subtle flaw, but another proof repairs it. The converse statement is true for a convex tangential quadrilateral: equal opposite sums do bring an incircle. The test checked 41 convex quadrilaterals with that property and found a point equally far from all four sides each time. If you drag a dot until the circle no longer sits inside the shape, Pitot's pair stops matching and instead AB + BC = CD + DA or AB + DA = BC + CD, as for an excircle.

The live cut-the-knot page now embeds a GeoGebra model rather than the Java applet; a 2005 Wayback capture of that same page embeds InscriptibleQuadri with ShowNames=0, and this port follows the applet's bytecode. One deliberate change: the applet chose the fourth dot at a random angle in [0, PI), which nearly always puts the circle outside the figure, so we start it at 4.6 radians where Pitot's equality is visible at once; the four switches keep the applet's unticked defaults. The Reset button and keeping drags inside the panel are presentation choices; the geometry itself is unchanged.

Tick Tangents and drag the dot P slowly round the circle: watch which pair of totals matches as the circle crosses out of the shape.
